I am a person who is a legalist, who honours legal institutions, and I can speak about all the things that are referred to in this note only with permission provided to me by the competent authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, in mid-2000, you were not in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, P8852. This is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Counsel, I apologise for the interruption. I apologise to counsel for the intervention, but I should alert the Trial Chamber, this witness is going to be asked -- I don't know what counsel has planned for the remainder of her cross-examination, but I can assure the Trial Chamber that it's the Prosecution's intention to conduct an extensive interrogation of this witness in respect of his activities as an operative for the Croatian government in 2000, in 1997, 1998, when he was attached to the Croatian embassy here in The Hague, and any number of other positions that he held after leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina during the time of the conflict. So I think that it -- maybe the Trial Chamber needs to sort this issue out now, because if the witness is going to decline to answer questions about these issues, then it's going to be our submission that his entire testimony should be stricken because we are not in a position to ask the witness legitimate questions that go to his credibility and his willingness to tell the truth in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you are raising a legal issue and in this courtroom I have no answer to give you. In many jurisdictions, in democratic countries, United States, France, or Croatia, operatives who work for the secret services are not authorised to talk about their activities unless -- well, first of all, they have to respect confidentiality. But in order not to be bound by confidentiality they need authorisations, and they can be -- end up by legal proceedings. And I think that this is the case in the United States, notably. So this is a new problem. Perhaps Mr. Karnavas has some light to shed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A couple of points. Couple of points, and let's be serious about it. First of all, first of all, we are talking about a period that is outside the indictment that the Prosecution wants to go into. Seconds of all, if we may recall the testimony of Galbraith who was heavily involved, heavily involved with the US government in shipping arms into Bosnia-Herzegovina at a time when there was an embargo, and it was clearly involved in the very thick of violating UN -- the UN embargo. Okay. And when pressed, his position was he couldn't speak about it. We also heard testimony from a Prosecution witness which we believe was an operative from one of the middle eastern countries, I'm not going name it because I don't want to indicate who the person was, but I think that we didn't press the issue because obviously it's an non-starter to start with. So I think that at this point in time, it may be good now that the Prosecution has indicated where it wishes to go, and I commend them for doing that, and I would agree that under other circumstances they may be entitled to pursue those lines of questioning, and if not that they can move for the entire testimony to be stricken. At this point in time, it may be useful to first excuse the witness from the courtroom, and then to have a brief discussion and to figure out where we are going to go from here. Because one, it would impact on the cross-examination of my colleagues, my cross-examination, if there is to be any, and I'm not suggesting that there will be one way or the other. But of course the Prosecution is entitled to have some, I would suspect, some guide-lines as to where it wishes to go, and the sooner the better as opposed to waiting until the end of the cross-examination by my colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's actually what I just wanted to say, Mr. Karnavas. I think, Ms. Alaburic, do you plan to go a lot into matters which the witness will probably say that he cannot answer, or will you -- do you have other areas which are negotiable? That are open terrain?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not ask the witness at all about his actives in the HIS. In the HIS, he worked from the autumn of 1994 until the first of March, 1995. And my question pertains to his activity in central Bosnia from September, 1992 up until the spring of 1994. I just used this official note as a basis for my question, but the question I am putting to him only pertain to his activity that he described during his examination-in-chief. My colleague, Senka Nozica, asked the witness about his activities as an SIS official, about his reports, about his activities in central Bosnia, and my question pertained to the same topics and the same period, and I do not intend to question the witness at all about what he did in the HIS. Perhaps, if some subjects related to the trial of General Blaskic crop up as interesting, I will just base my questions on newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but I should like to say something in relation to what the Prosecutor said. I want to have the witness's statement to be perfectly clear. He said that he was prepared to testify if he is given permission, because the Prosecutor said "if he is unwilling to testify." He said that he is perfectly willing to testify, but he has to get permission from the service that he worked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, unless I'm mistaken there are two separate issues here, there is the cross-examination by Ms. Alaburic which focused on his activities within the SIS, and then the Prosecutor is telling us that during his cross-examination he would like to ask questions on various activities that were carried out after the time when he was member of the SIS, and this is precisely where the problem lies. So the Judges will have to discuss it, we'll have to discuss it amongst ourselves. We'll see whether the Prosecutor will be allowed to ask the questions, but we are not yet there so we'll be able to discuss it beforehand. In order not to waste any time, I suggest that Ms. Alaburic carries on with her line of questioning which are not focused on the secret activities of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since the Prosecution will only start asking you questions tomorrow, so until then, could you perhaps contact representatives of your government in order to know whether you have the authorisation to tackle issues relating to your activities within the services that are covered by confidentiality in your country, and by tomorrow morning you might be able to tell us, Well, I was given the authorisation, I was not given such an authorisation, or I didn't get any answer. Is that possible at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate your interest and the interest of the Prosecutor, of course, concerning all these details, and I am prepared to discuss that at any point in time of course, and with the full consent of the competent authorities of the Republic of Croatia. I personally cannot -- I do not have the possibility to communicate during the course of the day with the competent authorities so that I could have this permission by tomorrow morning. I kindly ask you to understand me. As far as I am concerned personally, there is no obstacle whatsoever to my speaking about this and explaining this entire period; however, I do have to get permission from my authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to close the hearing at 13.45, so you have the entire afternoon to make a phone call to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Zagreb, you can mention the issue, they will get in touch with the presidency of the republic, and they will be able to let you know very quickly whether you have this authorisation or not. I'm not going to tell you how to do it. I'm just going to -- have just indicated how you could proceed, and then tomorrow morning you'll be in a position to let us know that this is what I did, this is what they said. Did you understand me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I shall do that. I shall do whatever I can to get the permission. I know what the course to be taken is so that I would get permission in writing to testify about all the facts that you are interested in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An additional question, when you came to testify here, did you ask your authorities an authorisation? I assume you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So when they authorised you to come, they knew that the Prosecutor would lead a cross-examination, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I assumed they did know. My testimony has to do about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the period is roughly 1991 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, I think that we have a bit of confusion there, perhaps I created it, but we have two different organs here. The witness did come here with a strictly formal permission provided for his testimony, and we had to do this in writing twice when he was supposed to come and testify here; however, we are not talking about the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that is supposed to give its permission or its consent. It's a different organ, a different authority that has to give its consent. So that's what the witness is referring to, this response in writing. So I don't think that he can resolve the matter just by phoning the foreign ministry. That is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, however, the witness is an expert and knows how to deal with such matters, because since the Prosecutor said that when cross-examining he will ask him questions about his credibility or he will test his credibility, and from what I understood he wants to ask him questions about his time at the Croatian embassy here in The Hague, therefore, he is bound to ask questions, and the witness could say No, I will not answer because this is closely linked to the diplomatic interests of my country. So this is a real issue which, of course, has to do with the Croatian foreign affairs ministry, but also Defence Ministry in terms of secret service activities. So the best for us is to ask Ms. Alaburic to carry on and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me before that, I would like to say something about the topic that we've been discussing to indicate how complex Mr. Bandic's situation is. I know roughly what the topic would be of Mr. Stringer's cross-examination. This is indeed something that has to do with his activity of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. However, in the Republic of Croatia, foreign policy is also within the province of work of the president of the republic, and of course in the interest of cooperating with the ICTY in the best possible way, the witness cannot theoretically communicate with all the authorities in charge and all the persons who are supposed to take part in making this decision. So could the witness, well, please try to do this, but if he does not manage to do it, it is due to these objective circumstances that I've just describe. In this context, can we just look at another document. The document is P8852.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 5 -- or, actually, let's say what the document is. It is the report of Major General Ljubo Cesic Rojs, dated the 21st of May, 1998, to the then Croatian President Dr. Franjo Tudjman, about what had happened at the 5th Sabor of the HDZ that was held on the 16th of May, 1998, in Mostar. We are not going to deal with all of this, but let us look at page 5 of the B/C/S text and page 9 of the English translation. It says that Bandic, that's you, is involved in key matters within the service as the chief of operations of SIS, and he is particularly engaged in operative work vis-a-vis central Bosnia, in parenthesis Kiseljak, Sarajevo. Tell us, is this statement in General Rojs' report correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by not correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, these are very arbitrary qualifications because these were political conflicts, and I really don't know anything about that, and I really did not -- I was not affected by it in any way because I was not politically engaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, I'm not asking you about the content of the document as a whole. I'm just asking you about this statement that I quoted in terms of your engagement in central Bosnia, Kiseljak Sarajevo specifically; is that part correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of the context is not correct because Mr. Rojs cannot know what my work was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We are not going to deal with this any longer then. Tell us, Mr. Bandic, did you personally ever write a report about your operative activities, and did you submit it to a commander or Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall ever having written something like that or that I was ever asked to do that. If I was asked to provide some information orally or some explanation, then I certainly did try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your interview to Globus that we looked at a few moments ago, 4D1652, that is the reference, in response to the direct question put by the journalist about the investigation concerning Stupni Do, you said that Petkovic did not order anything to me because he was not my superior; is that a correct statement, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It is correct in the sense of him not having ordered me to do anything and that's not the way our relationship functioned anyway. General Petkovic practically never gave me any orders. We had a relationship of confidence and friendship. If he ever required information about a particular case, I provided it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was General Petkovic your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes. Well, General Petkovic, as far as I understand things correctly, was certainly my superior. Not my immediate superior, but he was my superior because I was a military person, but he what not my immediate superior. That's how I understand it. He was my commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this a little. He was your commander. As an employee of the SIS, were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As you say that as of mid-1993 you were in the Main Staff, does that mean that General Praljak was your commander?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, General Praljak too, and General Petkovic also. I considered them my commanders. I was a member of the HVO and I wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the period we are dealing with regarding Stupni Do, Mr. Roso was the chief of the Main Staff, does that mean Mr. Roso was also your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately counsel, I consider the commander of the armed forces to be my commander. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, there's only one commander of the armed forces and that's the Supreme Commander, Mr. Mate Boban, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the armed forces also include the forces of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I'm not a military expert, believe me. I can't go into detail of the military structure. I only know the basics. But I'm not familiar with military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke about your communication with Mr. Ivica Lucic and the reports you wrote to him as the chief of the SIS. Did you consider Ivica Lucic to be your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to whom was Mr. Ivica Lucic responsible for his work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the head of defence who was his superior. Mr. Lucic was responsible to the head of the defence office, later the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bandic, let's look at this very briefly. In the Main Staff, was a post or section or department envisaged for SIS, General Praljak is telling me that he will deal with this more extensively, so just tell me according to the establishment of the Main Staff, according to any documents, can we find any trace that in the Main Staff, according to the establishment, there should be a staff member or a service of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I don't know what the detailed structure was. But I do know that Mr. Kraljevic, who succeeded me, was also a SIS employee in the Main Staff. How and through which establishment we were appointed there, I don't know, but physically there was an area, a space, a room there. First in Citluk and then in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, you are a lawyer, do you draw a distinction between the terms "employee in the Main Staff" and "employee at the Main Staff"? I wish to correct the interpretation. My question referred to employee in the Main Staff [In English] Attached to the Main Staff. [Interpretation] Do you draw a distinction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at my second set of documents, the last two documents. The first is 4D14324.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather 4D1324, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me, I can't find my way around this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of this second set, you have 4D1324, and Mr. Predrag Covic, who signed this document, is introducing himself as the officer for the SIS attached to the Main Staff, and the date is 26th of December, 1993. His name is Predrag Covic. Mr. Bandic, is this the same Predrag Covic which you mentioned as a SIS employee attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Madam Counsel, he is one of the three of us who were attached to the Main Staff. In addition to me, there was Mr. Covic and Mr. Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bandic, to whom did Mr. Covic send this report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the assistant of the minister, Mr. Biskic. I don't know who the other person is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the Main Staff is not among the addressees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's evident from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the introduction, the preamble. It says: "Pursuant to your oral order of the 26th of December," and so on and so forth, I visited the ground. So does it follow from this that Mr. Biskic issued an order to Mr. Covic for him to act on and that this is what this report is about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at 4D1325, that's also a piece of information by the same author, Mr. Covic, dated March 1994, and it's an assessment of the security situation in the Main Staff of the HVO. We don't have time to go into detail, but tell me, this Mr. Covic, is he in fact reporting on his, we could call it, security surveillance of the Main Staff, and is he informing his superiors in the SIS administration concerning the situation, the activities, and the problems in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I have never of course seen this document. I didn't see it at the time. I was not in the Main Staff of course. Mr. Covic was. It's unusual to see that there are no addressees here. I assume this is being sent to Mr. Lucic, that's the only way I can understand this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Employee of the SIS attached to the Main Staff, this term. Does it mean in fact that this employee is authorised to monitor the work of the Main Staff and report on the situation in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I don't know why you are so concerned with this in or attached to. I don't see what the difference is, but quite simply, he is authorised to compile information on the situation prevailing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the third set of documents. Witness, you told us when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] There is a problem, I'll resume. Let me put my question again. We've just seen a whole series of documents in which clearly the SIS is interested in the way the military apparatus quote unquote functions. The military brigade of the HVO is mentioned and the Main Staff of the HVO is mentioned. Based on this, I have the following question: The minister of defence, was he not the person that turned to the SIS to collect information on the way in which the military apparatus operated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot answer this question, although I would wish to be able to do so. I don't know whether he issued such an order, but certainly the chief of the SIS administration asked the SIS employee to compile such information. I don't know whether the head or the chief of the SIS administration -- well, I don't know who he got his orders from. I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, according to the regulations governing the work of the SIS, was it envisaged that the SIS had to deal with monitoring the situation in the HVO units and the military police units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the main tasks that the SIS dealt with, but I would wish to add, Madam Counsel, since you mention the military police, in the military police there was also the SIS which was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to the next topic. Mr. Bandic, you told us when we were reading one of the provisions governing the work of the security services, that in Herceg-Bosna, the regulations of the former intelligence services of the former state were copied more or less. Do you remember saying that answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to put to you some documents from which it clearly follows that in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the security administration was in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Do you know anything about the organisation of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I don't have the faintest idea of how the former army was organised. I was only trying to say that when these regulations were drawn up, the material from the former state was used, and the former military services, but also others in democratic countries of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bandic, do you know that the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina also had their security service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. But the HVO Main Staff did not have its own security administration, the security administration was within the Ministry of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us to the best of your knowledge, Mr. Bandic, the model according to which the SIS in Herceg-Bosna was organised? Was it similar or identical to the model according to which the SIS in the Republic of Croatia was organised?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In view of your answer, I won't waste time on comparing the regulations. Instead, I will put to you a statement made by the late Franjo Tudjman as the president of the state when he was conducting a conversation with officers of the Croatian army referring to the SIS, and I will ask you to comment on whether the same rule can be applied in Herceg-Bosna. The document is P131, 131. The transcript of the 4th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's good that you told me. Your Honours, as this is a large document, it is separate. It's been provided separately. So one of the documents is only this transcript. Witness, in the upper right-hand corner in the Croatian text you will find the following numbers, they are called ERN numbers, so look at the number ending in 948. And for Their Honours with respect to the text in English, it's 99 forward in the English text. So, Mr. Bandic, let's analyse this text. This refers in a way to the conflict between the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Main Staff of the Croatian army. Tell me, were you aware that in 1992 and 1993 there were some problems in delimiting the powers and authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not aware of that. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at this part. There are very many interesting details. I will have to cut this short. I hope I will do it in a fair way but anyone can read the document. It says, The minister also has part of my authority to administer the army and the Chief of the Main Staff to administer and the command, if I delegate that. And then I will skip over four -- or three or four paragraphs and I will go on. The SIS is under the minister here, down there it's under the commanders, but to the greatest extent, it is subordinated along the vertical line more than, let's say, operations and training. I will skip over a paragraph and go on quoting, So this means that the political sector of the personnel service, the moral and political and security service of the military police, and as regards the other services, the sectors of the ministry from securing the budget, procurement, and the supplies for the ministry, they have to deal with the Main Staff as a whole. And down there in the commanders also as a whole. Mr. Bandic, I conclude from this that the model was that at the state level the SIS is subordinated to the Ministry of Defence rather than the Main Staff, and the entire organisation should be such that SIS employees also work in the units of the Croatian army because their task is to monitor the situation in the Croatian army; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, my knowledge of this is minimal. I cannot assert with confidence how it was. President Tudjman was attempting to set up an organisation, but I am not familiar with this and I cannot draw any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, is that how it was in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be concluded that the model was similar, that it was attempted in a similar manner to transfer such things into Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the next document, 4D1310, part of an interview with Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, former HIS director. I'm interested in one answer, you can find it at the bottom of page 3. This is the only one that has been translated. It is dated 2000, a time when in Croatia new regulations on the security services were being introduced, and, prompted by that, the interviewer asks, How do you comment the proposed changes in military security and intelligent services. And Miroslav Tudjman answers, We see that there are HV Main Staff demands that the SIS is brought back under the wing of the Main Staff. This is a legacy of the JNA where KOS was under the Main Staff. This is something which belongs to the past. This was dealt with back in 1991 when those who are now trying to do so again, wanted for both the political department and the military police to be both the police -- military police, I correct myself, and the political department and the SIS be part of the General Staff. It is known, however, that because of a civilian oversight, this should be put into the Ministry of Defence system because this is a solution we can find in other western European countries. My question to you, Mr. Bandic, is, we've seen Army of Yugoslavia and Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who have security services within their Main Staffs. Is it true, is it correct that the Republic of Croatia and then Herceg-Bosna, modelled after the solution in Croatia, wanted for the Ministry of Defence, through the SIS, to conduct and preform civilian oversight over the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, after what you've read and after your question, I cannot answer by simply saying yes or no. I would like to appeal to the Bench to allow me to explain this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since I don't have much time, I would rather not dwell on the context, sir. Could you please answer whether SIS was a mechanism of civilian oversight over the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mechanism of civilian oversight over the military, well, I don't know the term.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The second row from the bottom, Miro Tudjman is discussing civilian oversights. Have you ever heard about civilian oversight?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Counsel, yes, of course. We are discussing a person who is an expert in security services. He was the head of security service of the Republic of Croatia. He is an expert in this field. That's one thing. Another thing, the relevant period is 2000, that's five years after the war. When Croatia had begun to build its democratic structures, and it's very difficult for me to draw any parallels between the statements of Professor Tudjman and the time and the circumstances prevailing when, in Herceg-Bosnia, the system was attempted to be created that would function.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, Mr. Tudjman discusses here the situation in 1991. He says that politically it has been overcome in 1991, and this is why I'm asking you this question, but we can proceed. Please take a look at the next document, 4D1308. At the same time, the then minister of defence who was a member of the liberal party says in the first paragraph that you can see in the left most column, The counter-intelligence or security part of the service is absolutely within the Ministry of Defence because of the possibilities for civilians oversight which is conducted through parliament, that is, through the Ministry of Defence. And this is why it is placed in the Ministry of Defence and so should be in Croatia. Please tell us, Mr. Bandic, this is the same matter, civilian oversight. Could you agree that security services are one of the ways whereby civilian authorities can exert control over the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I can agree that control is needed, absolutely, but again, this context is 2000, after profound political changes had occurred in Croatia, and the then minister of defence explains his position and opinion. I cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the time when Gojko Susak was minister of defence, were things different?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At the time I was not in position to define the relationships and how the relationship between the General Staff and the Ministry of Defence in Croatia were structured.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's skip one document and let's take a look at 4D1281. 4D1281. It is a schematic of the SIS, the Security information Service, which was drafted pursuant to a document referred to herein. Can we agree that the security sector, in that part which concerns the SIS, is -- consists of SIS administration and SIS centres in operational zones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that what is indicated, I hope that you have a colour print-out, the blue section, if not, you can see it on the screen in colour, can you agree that these are SIS operatives in military units in HVO units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When we see the lines, as the way they are connected, is it true -- I apologise, that the head of the Defence Department and assistant head of the Defence Department for security, or that is head of the SIS administration -- Mr. Bandic, can you repeat your answer to my previous question, whether this blue field denotes SIS operatives in military units as per operational zone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my understanding of this schematic, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that SIS operatives in the military units were appointed as per regulation and dismissed by the head of the Defence Department in cooperation with the head of the SIS administration and at lower level the head of SIS administration de jure or as per regulations; was that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: De jure, it was so, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So de jure by law, if a SIS operative failed to preform their duties conscientiously, head of the Defence Department could dismiss him, and at lower levels SIS administration head; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not concur. I think that this was at the commander level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the law, the letter of the law, de jure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's take a look at the rule book on the work of the SIS, which is a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, if my learned colleague wants to adduce this document as exhibit, let's have it at IC because we will be receiving it in black and white, but the witness has testified to the colouring of this document and this can open a door to misinterpretation. Could we have this document printed in colour as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, this document will always be in colour, and if you get hold of a colour printer, you will print it in colour. This document, after all, is an exhibit, and we used it when cross-examining Mr. Davor Marijan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I don't want to argue about that. But the question to the witness was whether the blue field denotes assistants SIS affairs of commanders. It's all about the context of the question and answer, and if my learned friend says it's in colour, then we will make sure that we use it as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, let's take a look at P4211. It's a rule book on the work of the SIS. Article 5 for starters. It says here, verification and control of the legality of work of the SIS is safeguarded and carried out by the head of the Defence Department and the commission appointed by the president of HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief, if I remember correctly, you said that you did not know whether the commission has been established at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether this means that head of the Defence Department was the only person who authorised to -- ensuring and implementing the verification and supervision of the legality of the work of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say so because I don't know whether the commission was set up. I don't know anything about the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Mr. Bandic, about the commission, but the competencies of the head of the Defence Department, pursuant to Article 5 of this rule book, which has been enacted by the head of the Defence Department himself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, it is clear from this provision that the head of the Defence Department and the commission do so, but I reiterate that I don't know whether that commission was ever established or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's take a look at Article 10 which says, The work of the administration shall be managed by its chief who shall be held accountable for its work and the work of the service to the head. Let's first agree on what the term "service" denotes. Could you please tell us, Mr. Bandic, whether we can define this term service as the SIS administration, SIS centres, and operatives of the SIS in military units and military institutions? Would that, put all together, would constitute the service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in its totality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In following from Article 10, if I'm reading this correctly, head chief of the SIS administration is responsible or accountable for the work of the whole service to the head of the Defence Department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can understand it by reading this provision, this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we said that the service is comprised of SIS operatives in military units, it means that the chief of the SIS administration is responsible to the head of the Defence Department for their work as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But the article states so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, counsel, in Article 7 mention is made of specialised security tasks. In Article 8, discusses information gathering, and Article 9 discusses what the operatives are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. But what about Article 10?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- what is known to me are military matters and expert matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will come to that, this is a completely different matter. Let's take a look at Article 11 then. It refers to SIS centres, and it states here that they coordinate and direct the work of all employees in their area. Please tell us, Mr. Bandic, whether this means that SIS centres are authorised to coordinate and direct the work of SIS operatives in the military units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I've just -- I've said that this coordinate and direct is the professional part of their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will come to that. Let's skip a large chunk, but we do not have the time to deal with everything, and let's take a look at Article 51. Let's check whether you defined correctly what the service comprises. In Article 51 it is state that all documentation shall be stored in the service administration, at SIS centres, and in possession of operative employees who, among other things, are part of the military units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I did not understand your question, because units are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Employees or operatives are mentioned and they are in units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Centres are referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we take a break or should I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest we go for a break now. You probably have one hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The hearing resumes, and before I give the floor back to Ms. Alaburic, I wanted to tell Mr. Stojic's Defence team the following. As you are aware of, tomorrow the witness will let us know what was the outcome of his proceedings with the authorities, but regardless of this, we ask the -- Mr. Stojic Defence team, by virtue of Rule 70, to hand in a request for protective measures in order to limit the scope of the cross-examination should it be necessary. So I invite you to do this so that when it comes to the scope of the cross-examination, you know precisely what is the position of the Croatian authorities, but it is up to you to do whatever needs to be done but you have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution position, but maybe I'm jumping the gun, but Rule 70 doesn't apply to this witness's testimony. He's already testified. He's already given evidence. There's been no confidential information that's been given to which Rule 70 might apply. So I -- certainly if they want to ask for protective measures at this extremely late time, Mr. Karnavas is right, this has been dealt with many other witnesses who come with a diplomatic background, but of course this is raised and dealt with and resolved by the Trial Chamber months in advance of any witnesses actually coming to testify here. So now this witness is going to go away tonight, and he is going to talk to some people at his embassy about the one thing he is not supposed to talk about with anybody, which is his testimony, so we are already running off the tracks, if I may suggest that, because of the fact that this issue was raised by the witness sitting in the stand for the first time while on cross-examination. So we are already in trouble, if I might suggest that. I think it's also incorrect, with respect, Mr. President, to suggest that Rule 70 applies at all to this witness's status or to the evidence that's already been given in open session. So if there are protective measures that will be sought, that's certainly fine, but it's not within the context of Rule 70, and certainly the Prosecution is going to take its own position in respect of the applicability of protective measures at this late stage of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, a very quick reply to the legal issue. There are many situations in the jurisprudence of this court where state's operatives benefitted from protective measures by virtue of Rule 70, General Clark being one example, and I could give you other examples. Secondly, you could -- you can benefit from protective measures at any time. Nothing stipulates that it has to be beforehand. It can be at any time. And thirdly, you said it yourself when you announced that you were intent on asking him questions on issues that haven't been tackled during the examination-in-chief or cross-examination. You, yourself, have -- the position originates from you. So the Trial Chamber has made its decision and has invited the Defence teams who invited the witness to come and testify to do have to is possible in order for this to be settled. Ms. Alaburic. Yes, witness, you raised your hand I hadn't seen you, I do apologise. Yes, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, thank you for giving me the floor. It does are to do me with me after all, so may I be allowed to be of assistance, if I can. I'm not asking for immunity here on account of my diplomatic status. That is not why I'm asking for a closed session. I'm not intervening because of that. I would just like to say that there are things regarding which I do not have permission. It is when I worked for the Croatian secret service. I cannot testify without the permission of the appropriate authorities. It's just a question of procedure. The answer will be there. I cannot call the president or the prime minister or the minister, Your Honours. Of course, they will respond to my call but there is a procedure that has to be abided by. I did not contact anyone so far. After I complete my testimony, I planned to meet up with my colleague, the ambassador here, since we are friends and we know each other but that would be after my testimony. Thank you for having allowed me to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, let us go back to our rules. Let us look at Article 62, the document is P4211. The rules on the work of SIS. Sorry, 63 actually. Article 63. Let us try to be as brief as possible. Article 63 says in paragraph 1: "Assistant commanders for SIS shall be required to perform the tasks of commanders of units within whose structure they belong which pertain to the scope of work of the service," as defined by the regulations. I'm trying to cut things as short as possible. Mr. Bandic, this provision shows that the SIS officers in military units are duty-bound to carry out the tasks assigned to them by the commander of the unit that they belong to; is that right.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next paragraph, With respect to the implementation of tasks from the scope of work of the SIS, the employees shall be responsible to the competent -- to the superior centre or administration. This provision shows that all SIS officers, including those in military units mentioned in the previous paragraph, shall be responsible for their work to the appropriate superior centre or administration; is that right, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the professional domain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the professional domain, are you actually referring to SIS work, that's what you meant by professional domain?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsellor, I'm trying to understand things and to explain them to you, and to me there is a double link. One is the military operative, one at battalion level, brigade level, military district level, so officers there are responsible to their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, sorry for interrupting, but please show me in this rule book where does it say that SIS officers in military units shall be responsible for their work to the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, that goes without saying. The commander is the one that issues orders within the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can I interpret your answer to mean that the rules do not stipulate this, but you believe that this goes without saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It goes without saying as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the same rules established that SIS officers shall be responsible to the centre or the administration, can you explain to us then how come this is regulated by these rules?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsellor, Your Honours, this was not my line of work. I really did not take part in the writing of these rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want detailed explanations of each and every article, you can always call a person who took part in this, who was simply in charge of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we are going to skip that. Let us look at paragraph 65 -- or rather, Article 65. Article 65 says the commander of a unit may issue an order to an employee of the SIS for the performance of tasks related to SIS work. Was that really the way it was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I said a few moments ago, as far as I'm concerned it goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next provision. The employee shall submit a report on the order executed not only to the commander who issued the order, but also to the centre or administration of the service. Is that the way it really was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsellor, I'm telling you once again, I did not write these provisions. We can interpret them. We can analyse them now. I'm familiar with the legal part, but I cannot tell you what things were like in the field. Things can be read the way you have read them just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you whether that's the way the things were in practice; namely, that a SIS officer in a military unit sent his report not only to the commander, but also to the superior centre or SIS administration. Is that the way things worked in practice as a rule, of course, not in each and every individual situation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. But it is possible that there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at Article 66 together. It says, In the event an order is issued to an employee of the SIS, which is beyond the scope of the work of the service, the employee shall immediately inform the person in charge in the SIS, and he, in turn, shall take appropriate measures prescribed by the decree in these rules. Tell me, Mr. Bandic, does this provision defend SIS members in military units from any kind of orders that would ask them to do something outside the scope of SIS work and that in such situations they can ask for protection from the person in charge of SIS, would that be the right way to interpret this provision?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at Article 68. It says, Employees of the SIS in commands and units shall inform the administration and centre in the prescribed manner about all developments influencing the state of security in counter-intelligence protection. Tell me, was that the way things were in practice, one of the tasks of SIS officers in military units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case, that it was one of the tasks. But I think that in practice it didn't really work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, to the best of your knowledge, did military commanders know that SIS officers had the task to report about the situation in the unit that they were in, that they were supposed to report to the centre or administration of the SIS, did military commanders know about that task? Did they know that SIS officers were sending report to the SIS administration or centre about the situation in that military unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know whether they knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I have prepared two more documents in this respect, however, in view of your answer who the members of the SIS were, I'm going to complete this topic that pertains to regulations and I'd like to move on to my next topic, and that is your statement, Mr. Bandic. If I understood you correctly, as you were answering the questions put to you by the Bruno Stojic Defence, you said that the appropriate procedure was not observed in the appointment of SIS members, and all the way up to sometime towards the end of 1993 SIS officers held their posts without having been appointed by authorised officials and in a way that was prescribed by the regulations. Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next number of documents after the blue piece of cardboard, document P938. Bruno Stojic, and command of the operative zone of central Bosnia in December 1992, appoints some high-ranking officers and among them number 12, Ante Sliskovic, head of security. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Bandic, how do you interpret this, does this document show that Mr. Sliskovic really held that position, that he was appointed to that position by Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsellor, this is the first time I see this document. Under number 12, head of security, this is a notion that I find confusing because as far as I know, Mr. Sliskovic was assistant head of SIS for the military district. I don't know what head of security means here, of the security centre that we've already discussed. We've already said that there were problems in its establishment up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, Mr. Ante Sliskovic was in the command of the operative zone, not at the SIS centre; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Please look at the next document, January 1993, Bruno Stojic. Dismisses from duty in the Banja Lukic Brigade from the positions of assistant commander for SIS and all duties and brigade logistics, the assistant commander. The document is P10306. P10306.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This document shows that Bruno Stojic could already in the beginning of 1993 relieve of duties SIS commanders in brigades. Did that really happen to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this is the first time I see this document yet again. What I find interesting is -- well, I don't know who Josip Maric was, although he was in SIS, although I had spent time there already, so according to this, yes, but I really do not know that this was a frequent occurrence. I really don't know. Especially I don't know who this man was. I personally find this interesting that I never came across him. I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P835 is the next document, let's have a look at it. This is a document on the appointment of persons to the Rama Brigade in Prozor. It's signed by Bruno Stojic, November of 1992. Point 3 says Luka Markesic is appointed head of security, chief of security. Tell us, Mr. Bandic, is that the same Luka Markesic that you spoke of during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's one in the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Please look at the next document. 2D1446. Again, this is a document signed by Bruno Stojic on appointment into the command of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade Krez Domagoj. It's a long decision. I'm just going to ask you to look at SIS officers very quickly now. Number 16 says Zarko Pavlovic, chief of SIS. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please help me once again.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it a bit illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 16, Zarko Pavlovic, chief of SIS.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that the same Zarko Pavlovic that you said during your examination-in-chief could not be resolved, is that one in the same person?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 17, look at that desk officer of SIS, Ljubo Ilic. Did you know this desk officer of SIS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I did know. The gentleman that we are talking about now, Mr. Ilic, that's someone that I do not know of and do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Number 65, Borislav Jurkovic, desk officer for security in the 1st Battalion. Tell us, did you know that security officer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I did not know him. Indeed, I did not have occasion to meet a great many people from different units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at number 94 now. Desk officer for security, Mile Tomic in the 2nd Battalion. Have you found him? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now for Their Honours and for the transcript, SIS desk officers are under numbers 124, 143, and 165. I'm trying to cut things as short as possible, so we are not going look at each and every one of them now. Tell me, Mr. Bandic, after these documents, could you at least change in part what you said during your direct examination, namely that desk -- that officers of SIS in military units were appointed by unauthorised officials apart from regular procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, there were many such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, if you were to count how many were appointed through a decision by Bruno Stojic and how many were not, could you give Their Honours at least a ball-park figure, because on the basis of your statement, it seemed that no one had been appointed in accordance with procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I never said that no one was appointed. I cannot give you a figure. I cannot give you a percentage, but yet again I would like to point out that after the administration was established, after we tried to establish centres in a way we worked on a recapitulation. We tried quite simply to compile a list to find out who these persons were, because these people had already been appointed for almost a year and a half. I mean, a year and a half before we tried to establish who the said officers were. There is a period that we are talking about because we had found a situation that we found --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Half a year, not a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we cut things as short as possible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to say that we found a certain situation, and only then was procedure observed and did they receive the kind of documents they were supposed to receive.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bandic, I would like to put a few questions to you now in relation to your answer given during the direct examination. In response to the question on whether SIS officers had the same kind of authority, like organs of the interior did in proceedings before district military courts. If I may be allowed to remind you, in response to the question put by the Bruno Stojic Defence, your answer was yes. After that the question was repeated and you changed your answer in the following way, you said that these duties of the organs of the interior before military district courts were enjoyed only by SIS members and military units, that is to say, that these responsibilities were not part of the responsibilities of SIS officers in the centre, and the administration. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. In the next set of documents, could you please look at document 4D1317. Again after the little blue cardboard. The first document there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a document that I prepared because I wanted to draw a comparison for you between the relevant provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure applied in the civilian judiciary and the provisions in military courts that apply in the military judiciary. So it's the first document after the next little blue cardboard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I cannot, well, it's a different document here, the one after the little blue cardboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Maybe you are looking at the wrong little blue cardboard. Yes, yes, look at that first page now. Yes, that's right. And now the next document. Do you see this document in two columns, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, we are going to give it to you. Yes, you can see it on your screen, yes, on your screen. You are a lawyer, Mr. Bandic, I think that you will be able to clarify certain matters for the Honourable Trial Chamber. On the left-hand side you have Article 148 of the criminal procedure act which discusses duties of all state organs, enterprises, to report criminal offences which are prosecuted ex officio. Please take a look at paragraph 3 of that article. It is said that: "State organs and enterprises and other institutions should in such criminal report to list evidence known to them," then they are duty-bound secondly to take measures to preserve traces of criminal offences, and thirdly, to safe-guard items which were the subject of or the instrument of commission of such criminal offence and other physical evidence. This was a piece of legislation in effect throughout former Yugoslavia, and you remember whether these were the duties of all the state organs, self-government organisations, et cetera, et cetera, I'm cutting a list short?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am a lawyer, but unfortunately, I did not deal with criminal law, but this is a provision known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at an identical provision which regulates these matters before military courts. It's Article 27 of a decree on military courts, which spells out the duties of commanders, military institutions, et cetera. The commander of a military unit must take all necessary measures to prevent the perpetrator of crime, to prevent his flight, to safe-guard physical items which may be used as evidence, and to collect all information that might be useful for criminal Prosecution and criminal proceedings, the military commander is duty-bound to inform the district military Prosecutor and the immediate superior officer of any such matters. Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this goes for a general obligation of the competent state or military organs to take whatever they can to help detect the perpetrators of criminal offences and help prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn the page. In Article 151 and 154, and there are some other articles, what is discussed is what organs of the interior are supposed to do with respect to criminal procedure. Your Honours, you may read it. These are typical activities of a police in any country which -- and they are authorised and duty-bound to perform such tasks. Let's list some of him. Detect and find perpetrator of a criminal offence, undertake measures to prevent his flight or him being unavailable, to secure evidence items which may be used as proof, collect all information which may be useful for a successful criminal prosecution, et cetera, et cetera. In the right-hand column, Article 25 on the Decree on military -- District Military Courts, it is said that the tasks of the interior shall be done by the authorised personnel of the security organ of the armed forces. This is what you discussed in your examination-in-chief, isn't that so, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your claim is, if I understood it correctly, that some SIS officers had authorities and powers of organs of the interior and some did not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Lawyer, my understanding of that is that in operative and military sense, and in this case as an authorised person within the security organ, together with the security assistant of the operation zone, it was their duty to act with respect to any criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you as an employee of the an SIS within the SIS administration did not have such powers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if I am in an immediate situation, and let me note for the benefit of the bench that I was such an authorised person in the previous regime in the ex-Yugoslavia, but I never had the powers of arrest, of apprehending and bringing in people, and I am discussing -- talking about pre-war period and the war period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But if I were to understand your testimony, you were authorised to talk where certain persons, for instance, those two who took part in the HVO action at Stupni Do, you were authorised to make an official note, to forward that official note to your superior, Ivica Lucic, for further procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had authority to conduct interviews and produce a note, maybe just -- maybe even take a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Article 151, Criminal Procedure Act. The powers of the organs of the interior are defined as such to collect information from citizens to search in appropriate matter, to collect evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene, I apologise. I would like the witness not to be implied or imputed. He said that he had powers to interview and produce an official note, and this Article 151, paragraph 2, discusses what the official organs of the interior had powers to do. As far as I can understand, the witness in examination-in-chief said exactly that, it was envisaged that organs of the interior could investigate and everything else that SIS organs had no authority to do, neither did they have capacity to do it. So if it is imputed that he had said that, then let's read out paragraph 2 of Article 151 to see what organs of the interior did in connection with documenting criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What my colleague is saying, she is going to deal with in her redirect. I'm not going to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you my concluding question with respect to this. So your thesis is that SIS administration was not in charge of the detecting crimes, criminal offences, collecting evidence, and submitting and lodging criminal reports and criminal prosecution and initiating criminal proceedings against perpetrators. Is this your thesis?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, P128. It is a report on the work for 1992. The part which concerns the SIS.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Lawyer, could you assist me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document following this juxtaposed overview immediately after the document that you have in your hands, the next -- the very next document. On page 8, this is a report covering 1992, a report on work of the HVO. On page 8 is a section of the report which concerns the SIS, Security and Information Service. In English, I will give you the page number very soon, unfortunately I haven't noted it. Mr. Bandic, please take a look. It is stated here towards the end of the second paragraph, midway down the page, After systematising, analysing data which are collected through operational work and through interviews, consolidated reports were produced for the head of the Defence Department and the president of the HZ-HB. Have you found this part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In English, it's also page 8, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no pagination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Take a look at the screen, please, the last paragraph, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not discussing the same document. There's no pagination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, please be kind and focus on the screen. The last sentence in this first large paragraph saying: "After systematising and analysing data collected through operative work and through interviews, consolidated reports were produced for the head of the Defence Department and the president of HZ-HB." Have you found this, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, systematising and analysing data gathered through operations, could you please tell us what activities these are referred to. How is this done, how do you collect or gather data through operations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simple, madam counsel, and this is the work that is the basis for our service. If somebody submits a document through a connection or an informant, then this is operations, and then through interviews by producing official notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Interviews. This is what -- we saw that organs of the interior are authorised under the Criminal Procedure Act, they are authorised to interview and talk to citizens, see if they have some knowledge about certain criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says here that comprehensive reports were made by the SIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And following from this report it, says that such comprehensive reports were submitted to the head of the Defence Department and president of the HZ-HB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If this is stated here, I can just confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip one paragraph. Please take a look at the paragraph which is at the bottom of that page. The part which said that the service, in accordance with its capability, it has also participated in the monitoring and detection of organised crime, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, this is a part of the report which was drafted by the SIS administration. If it's true what you said, that SIS administration was not in charge of activities concerning the detection and prosecuting criminal offences, how come that this claim has found its way to this SIS administration's report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam counsel, my understanding is simple. It says here the service, and this is referring to the whole service, criminal offences are referred to about which the service collected and analysed data, but the data came from the field through the centres, et cetera. When I said the administration, please understand me that I'm referring to ten people or so who have no capability of going out in the field. This was a place where we tried through operational and analytical work to cover this part of our responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Bandic, SIS operatives and employees at the SIS administration did not conduct operative work in the field, but they processed the data they received from the ground concerning prosecution of criminal offences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not just that exclusively. I did go out in the field personally, but I'm talking about the administrative and operational capacities. I want to avoid you understanding that there was a large number of people who could work also in the field, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But from your answer, it follows that you at times would go out in the field and collect information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I collected such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: SIS employees at SIS centres, they were closer to what was going on on the ground than people in the SIS administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was of course so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us whether they collected evidence in the field and tried to contribute to successful detection and prosecution of perpetrators of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of their tasks. One of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's take a look at the next document. Mr. Bandic, I think it is in a separate set of documents, there are three documents because of their volume were set aside. This is P4699. It's a HVO work report for the first half of 1993. I'd like to draw your attention to the SIS administration's report which starts on page 17 of the Croatian version. Please take a look at page 18. There is a very important remark, one of the key topics in this whole trial in the opinion of General Petkovic's Defence team. Have you found it? In English version that's page 11.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The service in a timely manner registered many irregularities within HVO units, skipping the rest of the sentence. And I'm quoting the next sentence, As a separate problem in certain units, we found a large number of troops, non-Croats who were mainly Muslims. The importance of this warning was confirmed when the ABiH army attacked the HVO at Bioelo Polje when HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity walked over to the ABiH ranks and were the strongest force of the Muslim army in the attack against Grbavica. My question is, was the HVO created as a military force of Croats, Muslims, or all citizens or citizens without any ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question, Madam Counsel, is -- touches the main topic, but it necessitates a wider elaboration, and it necessitates an explanation of how things came to a head in this way that it was described here. By the Bench's leave, I would delve into a wider explanation, this is a very delicate political matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, I fully agree with you, and I think it would be very good to do that if we had sufficient time. But all I'm interested in at this point is what your perception was. Did the authorities in Herceg-Bosna truly wish to create the HVO as the giant army of the Croats and Muslims, was it a multinational, multiethnic army up until mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the HVO as a multinational army. And the army of BH also had different nationalities in it at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you can continue tomorrow, you have time left, and the Registrar will tell us how much time you actually have. We would just like to complete the oral decision that was handed down this morning as regards the cross-examination that will be conducted by the Prosecution. I shall read this out slowly so that no mistakes are made. Let me stipulate, Ms. Alaburic, that you will have 26 minutes left for tomorrow. The Trial Chamber in its oral decision completes the already -- the decision that has already been handed down as follows. The Trial Chamber, after having recorded the comments made by the Prosecution and the witness's statement, would like to complete the oral decision in the following manner: Asking, thereby, the Stojic Defence team to carry out the necessary measures on behalf of the witness since the witness is a witness of the court, and according to the response provided by the Croatian authorities, to seize us of a motion pursuant to Rule 70 of our rules of procedure if necessary. To sum up, Ms. Nozica and Mr. Khan, it's for you to phone up the authorities in question because the witness is now in a position where he is a witness of the court. We have addressed matters of substance and therefore he cannot discuss a case file with his authorities. But you may, and you can therefore call up the authorities and explain the problem to them. If the authorities have nothing against this witness talking about his activities which he had after he worked for the SIS. So please file a written motion pursuant to Rule 70 of our rules, please. The witness, therefore, will not find himself in a delicate position. Witness, I'm sure you've understood what I've just said. You musn't phone anyone up since you are now a witness of the court, and we do not wish to put you in a delicate position. The lawyers that have asked you to come and testify will do that on your behalf. They have all afternoon and all night to do so. We will now adjourn and meet again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
